45th ANNUAL REPORT. 


As the pioneer of all the Associations on this Continent, now 
numbering 300,000 members, this Association has stood, for the past 
45 years, with its doors wide open and its hands outstretched to help 
young men of the City of Montreal to higher and better things in the 
struggle of life. We bear testimony to God’s great goodness in the 
past, and we would offer profound thanksgiving for the privileges 
and opportunities accorded to us in this work. 

No thoughtful, conscientious man could possibly see, during the 
past fall and winter, from 500 to $00 young men passing through 
the Building and distributing themselves in the various rooms, 
attracted thither by some one of the practical and helpful 
agencies which our work offers, without being deeply impressed 
by the far-reaching influence of this work, and its growing value 
to the city and country. That the doors of this beautiful building 
swing open for 14 hours each day in the year to the touch of 
any young man who is ambitious to add to his talents, or having 
fallen in the race, longs to recover himself and make a new Start in 
life, must surely be a source of deep gratification to all those 
who have had any part in its erection and maintenance. 

The preventive and constructive work of the Young Men’s 
Christian Association occupies a large part of its time and effort ; but 
it always carries an open hand for the rescue and reformatory work, 
as so many bright instances each year bear testimony. Reform and 
relief work, as a tule, secures the greatest sympathy from the 
public ; yet how much easier and cheaper and infinitely better it is to 
keep young men from going wrong, and to build them up in true 
Christian manhood than it is to try and reform them after they have 
gone astray, and destroyed the most forceful part of their lives. 


10 


A few facts concerning the work of the year will show the extent 
and variety of the different classes reached, and the SPPOreasiiss 
which this Building presents :— 

201,450 visits by young men to the Association Building exclusive 
of meetings. 

6,270 persons attended the practical talks, lectures and social 
gatherings. 

10,706 young men attended the Bible classes and religious 
meetings of various kinds. 

372 classes for physical exercise were conducted by the Physical 
Director and Assistants, with a total attendance of 5,590 young men. 

500 young men make use of the gymnasium, swimming bath, 
bowling allevs and physical privileges weekly. 

347 Evening Educational Classes, where instruction could be 
secured in thirteen different branches, were held, with an enrolment 
of 356 individual students. 

7,347 books were drawn from the Library by 545 readers. Our 
Library only contains 3,500 volumes. 

The Reading Room contains 140 Periodicals and Magazines, and 
is used daily by an average of 275 young men. 

378 young men were counselled and helped regarding employment. 

451 new members were admitted during the year. 

The total membership at the close of the year, including Juniors, 
was 1,662. | 

The Junior, Department has I69 members. It has maintained 
religious meetings and Bible classes, with a total attendance of 
2,380 boys. Separate Reading Room, Library, Social and Physical 
work carried on by a carefully planned organization amongst the 
boys themselves. 

Bicycle, Lacrosse, Football, Snow-shoe and Chess Clubs have 
been maintained amongst the members. 

In July and August the Association carries on a camp at Lac 
St. Joseph, near St. Agathe, for the use of the members on their 
vacation. 

Hundreds of young men have been counselled in reference to 


i 


their Christian life, and many of these are now active in Church or 
Association work. 

The Building has become increasingly a centre for many kinds of 
meetings and interests connected with the educational, temperance, 
Christian and philanthropic work of the city. 

The cost of the work for the past year, running seven days 
each week and evenings, has been $13,618.34. The cost per 
member was $9.64. Of this cost the member gave an average 
in fees of one dollar for every dollar given by friends. This is true 
philanthropy—helping young men to help themselves. 


BRANCHES. 


The development of this work at one central point can never take 
the place of branch organizations, wisely located in different sections 
of the city. The electric cars are fast taking the young men beyond 
the reach of the Central Building for satisfactory evening work. 
They cannot return in time, besides the barrier of the additional 
expense involved. There is no doubt that the conservative policy 
of the Association during the past few years, in refusing to extend 
until the necessary funds were placed in their hands for that purpose, 
has been a wise one, especially in view of the financial depression 
which has prevailed. But we fail to understand why some broad- 
minded citizen does not come forward and seize this unparallelled 
opportunity for an investment which must bring great returns. That 
such men are in this city there is no room to doubt. We again 
bring this matter before the public, presenting the opportunity as it 
appears tous. The city of Pittsburg has five branches; St. Louis, 
four; Milwaukee, three; Detroit, three; Chicago, eight; and New 
York, fourteen branches where the work of the~ Association 
is carried on. Through the late Mr. Samuel Inslee, the latter 
Association recently received an office building on Broadway valued 
at $200,000, the receipts from tenants to be used for the current 
expenses of the Association. We hope this year will not close 
without some provision for the extension of this work in other 


sections of the city. 


12 


The Annex for our present Building still remains unbuilt. This is 
an opportunity for some citizen interested in educational work to 
invest $30,000 to good purpose. 

Prominent among the events of the year we mention: 

Frrst.—The great loss which our Association has sustained 
through the death of our much beloved Treasurer, Mr. Warden King, 
in July last. He was a member of the Association since 1856, but 
he came on the Board of Management at a time when the Associa- 
tion was in great difficulties, and continued as a most active worker 
until his death He did much to secure for the Association that 
measure of confidence in the eyes of the public which it had in the 
erection of its present Building, and his personal influence on the 
Board of Directors was most helpful to the other members. In his 
will he left the Association $5,000 

Srconp.— Changes have been made in the Executive force. In 
September, Mr. P. H. Cushing, Assistant Secretary in charge of the 
Junior Department, resigned to enter the Springfield Training 
School. Mr. C.K. Calhoun, formerly Assistant Secretary at Toronto, 
and Secretary at Lindsay, Ont., was secured, and has filled this 
position acceptably to the Board. Mr. A. H. Ellerbeck was secured 
as Librarian in place of Mr, R. H. Judd, who returned to England. 
Mr. C. B Powter was secured as Assistant to the Physical Director. 

TuHirpD.—The Building was entirely tinted last summer, giving its 
interior quite a new appearance. The part set aside for rental has 
been well filled. The deficiency on the Property Account has only 
been $488.08, as against $1,140 last year. After the payment 
of £1,000 on June 1, the mortgage indebtedness will still be 
#,10,500. If this could only be reduced to $25,000 the excess 
of revenue on Property Account would then be sufficient to carry the 
running expenses of the first Branch of the Association. One of 
the objects in the erection of this Building was that its rented 
portion should at some time meet the extra expense needed to carry 
on the Association work at two additional points in the city. 


MEMBERSHIP. 


The membership is the central point. We have not definitely 
organized this branch so as to secure the best results. This has 
been a mistake. We hope to do so this year by securing a 
Committee that will meet each week, as the Finance Committee 
meet, and carry forward a well organized canvass throughout the 
city. We should make the membership 2,000 before next Annual 
Rteerlng: In securing new members, the most effective method of 
advertising is through the personal words or influence Go tare 
members themselves. By keeping each Department ‘up to date” 
the privileges of the Association, when properly presented, are sure 
to draw young men, and it is the young men we need. Every other 
Department will come into line, and keep pace, if the Building 1s 
kept constantly filled with young men. Let us make this the 
central work for the new year. Every member can serve here. 
Volunteers are called for. We have to report one Life Membership 


this year of 100. 


COMMITTEE FORCE. 


This is essentially a work for young men by young men. If 
‘t fails to develop a constant, increasing volunteer working force 
from among its members, but adds to its official staff, it will be 
proportionately weak and inoperative. The Committee organization 
is a great educator. The voluntary co-operation and self-sacrificing 
services of 136 Committee men has made possible the results 
presented to-night in the various reports which follow. From the 
office standpoint, we wish to thank these young men who have 
so cheerfully given their time and effort. But we should have 
at least 250 Committee men. The work demands it. You need it. 
If you can only give one night each week, or one night each fort- 
night, or one night each month, come and volunteer your services. 
We can use you in some place. Our President has issued a letter to 
a large number of the active members, enclosing an outline of 
our Committee organization, asking their co-operation. We hope 
there will be a prompt and hearty response. 


14 


Prominent amongst the Committees is the Finance Committee. 
The general depression in business has added to the difficulties 
of their task, but they have labored with renewed earnestness, and 
to-night present a gratifying report. To the Chairman, Mr. D. W- 
Koss, and the Treasurer, Mr. L. H. Packard, and each member of 
the Committee, the thanks of the whole Association is due. 

The past year an Association Orchestra has been added, which has 
been of great service on both the social and religious sides of 
the work. We are indebted to Prof. Cathcart Wallace for his able 
leadership, and Mr. C. W. Brown for his interest in this important 
branch. ‘They promise increased efficiency for next fall and winter 
work. During summer months a public recital will be: given in the 
Reception Hall every alternate Thursday evening for the benefit of 
the members and their friends. . 

The reports of the various Departments are presented to-night in 
detail. We ask for their careful consideration by each member. 
Perhaps there are but few persons who realize the magnitude of the 
work carried on in this great Building, and the issues which go forth 
year by year. The centre of the whole is the 


RELIGIOUS WORK, 


Informal religious services for men, to the number of 260, have 
been held, where the great facts of Jesus Christ as a personal Saviour 
from sin, and His power to enable men to lead a new life, have been 
presented. Scores of men have been led to accept this great 
foundation truth, and have been shielded from temptation, especially 
during their early residence in the city. Apart from these definite 
meetings, a Christian atmosphere has pervaded the whole and 
hundreds of young men have been counselled and personally dealt 
with during the daily routine. In addition to the meetings in the 
Building, services have been held each week in the General Hospital. 

We would name two special needs, First—A well organized 
Committee to carry on a Men's Meeting Sunday afternoon which 
would reach ‘‘outsiders,” and tell effectually in the city. Second—A 
series of well planned Training Classes for workers. We hope both 
of these will be carried out in the new year. 


15 
DISTRICT WORK. 


This is a new department. The young men from the country are 
now crowding into the city centres so rapidly that the Association is 
seeking to secure a correspondent in each town and village in our 
Province who will be advertised in the community, as such, and 
whose work it will be to see that every young man leaving his section 
and coming to this city or any other city, carries with him a letter of 
introduction to the Secretary of the Association. Already we have 
secured 15 such correspondents, and hope to see a Committee 
formed who will push the work during this year. Each of these 
places should have a delegation visit from members of this Asso- 
ciation. 

The past years work has been very greatly aided by the hearty and 
generous co-operation of the ladies of the various churches. We 
here record our ovligations to them. 


IN MEMORIAM. 


We have to record the following list of subscribers who have been 
taken from amongst us by death during the year :— 

E. F. AMES~A member since 1865, and a member of the Board of 
Trustees during and for many years after the erection of 
the Victoria Square Building. 

G. E. JAQguEs—A member since 1863, and for many years on the 
Committee of Management in the Victoria Square Building. 

WARDEN KtNG—A member since 1856, and Treasurer at the time of 
his death. 

Roptr. L. GAutr—A subscriber to the Association since entering the 
Dominion Square Building in 1890. 

Ropr. ANDERSON 


A member of the Association since 1865, and a 
constant contributor to its expenses. In his will he 
bequeathed $2,000 to the Association, the interest upon 
which is to be used for its mission work. 


16 


As we close this report we record our thankfulness to God for the 
privilege of service for our fellow young men, for Christ’s sake. We 
confess the faithlessness and failures of the past year. But we enter 
the new year with renewed confidence in Him, and also in the 
citizens of Montreal who are interested in the welfare of their young 
men, and have faith to believe that the Association will be crowned 
with richer and more abundant blessings than it has ever known. 


D. A. BUDGE, 
Secrelary. 


17 


FINANCE. 


The Finance Committee, in common with those who had the financial responsi- 
bility for other benevolent institutions, have found the past year a difficult one ; but 
through the assistance of kind friends, who contributed additional funds to meet the 
apparent deficit, the year has been closed without debt. The gratitude of the 
Association is surely due to all who have contributed to that end. 

The floating debt on the building has been wiped out, and £1,000 has been paid 
on the mortgage debt. Before this report is printed the mortgage will be reduced 
by another £1,000, and will then amount to £10,500. 

The Trustees of the Estate of the late Robert Anderson have advised the Associa- 


tion of a bequest of $2,000, which will probably be available during the coming year. 


D. W. ROSS, 


Chairman.

SUBSCRIPTIONS. 


The following list includes no membership fees except those paid by Sustaining 
Members, who are indicated by an asterisk (*). A large number of Full and Limited 
Members pay their fee simply as a recognition of their interest in the work, but it is 
impossible to indicate them without publishing the membership roll, for which we 
have not space. They will please accept our most hearty thanks. 

Amounts marked ‘‘e” were special offerings made at Easter. Amounts marked 
“d” were class deposits donated to the Educational Department.

EDUCATIONAL DEPARTMENT. 


This Department offers thorough practical instruction in those branches which 
will assist a young man to decide upon his life-work, or help him in the business or 
trade in which he is employed. It appeals to that large class of young men 
who have been deprived of the opportunity for a complete education, and who 
though busy during the day are willing to spend their evenings in that training 
of the head and hand which will make them-more efficient. The subjects taught 
give practical earning power as well as general culture. The outlines herewith given 
indicate briefly the scope of the work attempted, and show how practical and com- 
prehensive the courses are. Three hundred and fifty-six individual students have 


secured instruction in ¢Azrteex.subjects. |

AGASSIZ SOCIETY. 


The natural history collection of the Cote St. Antoine Branch of the Agassiz Asso- 
ciation was donated to the Young Men’s Association early last year. It was decided, 
among the members interested in this branch of study, to reorganize, and if possible 
carry on the work under the old charter. After some correspondence with Mr. H. H. 
Ballard, President of the Association, the matter was arranged, and the reorganization 
was completed on June 4th, 1895. 

The Society at present consists of 30 resident members and one corresponding 
member. Ten monthly meetings have been held 3 average attendance, eight. 

The Society gave eight lectures, during the season, on various subjects of natural 
history, which were well attended, and much enjoyed by the members. The lectures 


were as follows :— 


1895. June 14. ‘‘ How to Begin.” - By Dr. Deeks. 


Oct. 18. ‘*Some Facts on Plant Life.” By Mr. H. Cushing, 
of McGill College. 


Nov. 22. ‘‘ The Honey Bee.” By Mr. C. T. Williams. 

Oct. 27, ‘‘Introduction to the Fly Family.” By Mit. C. T: 
Williams. 

1896. Jan. 31. ‘‘ Spiders.” By Mr. C. T. Williams. 4 

Feb. 14. “‘ Volcanoes.” By Prof. Adams, of McGill College. 

April 7. “ Birds In and Around Montreal.” By Mr. J. B. 
Williams. ) 

May 14. ‘‘ Wild Flowers from Mount Royal.” By Mr. H. 
Cushing, of McGill College. 


ol 


The Executive are already planning a regular course of lectures on natural history 
or next winter : also one or two evenings with the microscope. During the summer 
the Society propose holding one or two outings on Saturday afternoons to points of 
‘nterest around Montreal. These outings are of great advantage to the members, 
enabling them to put in practice what they have learned during the winter. 


The following are the officers for the year 1896 :—

The accustomed care has been bestowed upon the maintenance of these two 
important and popular features of the work, and it is satisfactory to record that the 
abundant use made of them by the members bespeaks a hearty appreciation of the 
benefits provided. 

The total expenditure upon both departments fell slightly short of $500, . this 
amount being about’equally'divided *between them.

RELIGIOUS DEPARTMENT. 


YOUNG MEN’S MEETING. 

Fifty-two Young Men’s Meetings have been held during the year. The attendance 
ranged from 45 to 120, with an average for the year of 64. At more than one-half of 
the meetings there have been young men making personal inquiry concerning the 
Christian life, and these have been personally dealt with by the members and officers. 
The Committee has planned three months’ courses of topics in advance, and chosen 
leaders who have presented Christian truth in its practical bearing upon young 
men’s lives. We feel sure that God’s Word will not return unto Him void. We 
feel confident that this meeting has been especially an educator in the lives of many 
young men who have just been beginning in the Christian life. The opportunity for 
personal testimony has been especially helpful on this line. 

The Committee suffered a great loss during the year in the removal of its faithful 
Chairman, Mr. James Greig, to Cardinal, Ont. He was a consecrated worker, 
and the whole Association has met a loss in his departure. He carries with him the 
best wishes of the workers. 

We enjoyed the helpful service of Mr. Fred. Meyers as leader of the Service 
of Song for part of the time ; but his choir duties compelled him to give itup. We 
very greatly need a consecrated leader of the singing, or a quartette who would take 


charge of the Song Service here. 


Ai. We PAYIRE, 
Secretary. 


34 


THE YOUNG MEN'S BIBLE STUDY. 


Your Committee have much pleasure in submittiug the following report for 
i the year just closed. 

) The Class has had an aggregate attendance of 3,559, the weekly average being 69, 
which is very encouraging, considering that for several Sundays during the winter 
severe storms prevented a full attendance. Some Sundays we have had over one 
i hundred present, showing the interest taken by our members in this most important 
' part of our work. 

The studies have been from the conversations of our Lord, and have proved of much 
i benefit to the members, not only to the Christian young men, but also to those who 
were out of Christ, as a large number have testified to their acceptance of Christ and 
are now leading consistent lives. 

An Invitation Committee has been added, which has done good work, and many 
have been brought in by this means. The annual Class Tea was held on December 
29th, 89, being present. The testimonies at that time were most encouraging. 

Letters have been received from members in the following piaces, who have 
| removed from the city, viz.: Scotland, England, Jamaica, Ottawa, Peterboro, Ont., 
i and a number of other places, all speaking of the benefit received while attending the 
Class. 

The Committee pledged themselves to remember the Class each day in prayer 

i during the hour of twelve to one. 
i‘ We desire to thank the following ladies and gentlemen who have assisfed us in the 
i! music, viz.: Mrs. D. W. Ross, Mrs. Kingman and Miss Schneider, and Messrs. 
4 J. Ritchie Bell, W. T. Walmsley, J. J. Lomax, and the Association Orchestra under 
aM the leadership of Prof. Cathcart Wallace, also the following who have led the Class 
ih during the absence of Mr. Budge :—Rev. Mr. Scott, and Messrs. Chas. T. Williams, 
W. F. Chapman and C. K. Calhoun. 


ALEC. ARTHUR, 


Chatrman. 
SPECIAL BIBLE STUDY COURSE. 


The Tuesday evenings from October to March were set apart for a Special Bible 
Study Course, which would be of practical value to our workers. The Committee 
secured the following teachers and topics :— 


Oct. 8.—‘*‘ How We Came by Our English Bible.” 

Rev. Dr. Barbour, Prin. Congregational College. 
if ‘* 22,‘* The Inspiration of the Bible.” 
i Rev. Dr. Barbour. 
Hee ‘¢ 29-Nov. 19.—Four Lessons—‘‘ Outline of the Old Testament.” 

Rev. Prof. Scrimger. 
Nov. 26-Dec. 10.—Three Lessons—‘‘ Outline of the New Testament.” 

Rev. A. M. Phillips, Douglas Church. 
Jan. 21-Feb. 11.—Three Lessons—‘‘ Office and Work of the Holy Spirit.” 

Rev. G. Osborne Troop, St. Martin’s Church. 
Feb. 18—-March 3.—Three Lessons—‘‘ How "to Study the Bible for Personal 
i Growth and Use with Others,” and “ Methods of Bible Marking.” , 
H Mr. Fred. Meyers. 


30 


The attendance averaged 35 young men, and they testified publicly and privately 
to the benefits they received. We wish to thank these gentlemen for the time 
and effort they gave to this work. We would suggest that a Course of Bible Studies 
on ‘*The Deepening of the Christian Life,” by a suitable leader would be most 


helpful for the early Fall work. 
Rk. L. CHARLTON, 


Chairman. 
MEN’S MEETING. 


This meeting for men was held on 25 Sunday afternoons during the fall and 
winter. The following gentlemen have given addresses :-— 


Bishop Baldwin, of Huron. 

Canon Dumoulin, Toronto. 

Bishop Courtney, Nova Scotia. 

J. A. M. Aikins, Winnipeg, Man. 

Rev. David Heron, American Missionary. 
W. H. Williams, Evangelist. 

Rev. W. Hay Aitken, of England. 


Eugene Stock, London, England. 

David McConaughy, Madras, India. 
Claus Olandt, Jr., New York. 

Sir William Dawson. 

Rev. Dr. Clarke, Missionary to Bulgaria. 
Rev. Dr. Rose, City. 

Miss Ben Oliel, Jerusalem. 

Dr. Lyman B. Sperry, Boston, and others. 


The Service of Song was led by Mr. J. Marshall Williams, of St. James Methodist 
Church. 

These addresses have been listened to by an average of 135 young men, and 
while the meeting is not of that character where you can see direct results, your 
Committee are sure that these addresses have deepened the religious convictions 


in the minds and hearts of many. 
J. HAMILTON FERNS, 


Chairman. 


SUNDAY MORNING BIBLE CLASS. 


From May Ist until Dec. 31st were occupied in studying two series of very inter- 
esting and profitable lessons, the first consisting of the most familiar of the Psalms, 
and the second of the Beatitudes in Matthew v. 1-12. Since Jan. Ist Mr. Geo. H. 
Archibald has very kindly led the Class in the study of the International S.S. 
Lessons. Mr. Archibald’s methods of teaching and illustration have been very 
helpful, especially to those engaged in teaching in the Sunday-schools. The 
attendance for the year has been as follows: Number of Sessions, 50; total attend- 
ance, 751 3 average, I5. 

W. F. CHAPMAN, 
Chairman. 


36 
INVITATION, 


This Conimittee has done invitation work in connection with the Saturday night 
meeting by standing on the principal street corners and handing an invitation card to 
the young men whom they may meet. They have been able to do this each Saturday 
during the year with an average attendance of 5 members. ‘They have also assisted 
at invitation work in connection with the Sunday afternoon meeting when any special 
speaker was announced, and about .21,900 invitations have been handed out during 
the year. | | 

The Committee have to regret the removal of several of its members, and 
others have been unable to attend, so that we have had, from time to time, to. 
add new workers, for whom the Committee offers an excellent opportunity. 

The work is encouraging and helpful, not only to those who are persuaded to come 
to the meetings and have received benefits from them, but also to the members of the 
Committee. The presenting of an invitation card in many cases gives an opportunity 
for personal invitation, and is, therefore, a field for useful and profitable work for 


every young man who would engage in the cause of Christ. 
W.. A. GRAY, 


Chairman. 
SOCIAL DEPARTMENT. 


The Committee in charge of the Social and Reception Department for the year 
1895-96 beg to report as follows :— 

In order, more thoroughly, to cover the work, it was considered advisable to divide 
the Department into four Committees, viz. :— 

1. A Committee in charge of the Sunday Evening Tea for Strangers. 

2. A Committee on Committee Men’s Reunions. 

3. A Committee on Members’ Socials. 

4. A Reception Committee. 

STRANGERS’ TEAS.—Five Strangers’ Teas have been held, with an average 
attendance of twenty-three. These are held usually on the first Sunday 
evening of each month at 5.30, and are for the benefit of young men: 
who have lately come to the city. One of the Directors presides, and after 
tea a service of song is held in the parlors with reading a portion of Scripture’ — 
and prayer, and is closed in time to allow the members to attend whatever 
church they may desire. It was the intention of the Committee to hold one of these 
meetings each month, but being unable to secure sufficient names, two or three of the 
months were passed over. The expressions of a large number of the strangers who 
accepted invitations indicated the pleasure they enjoyed at being present, and 
we trust that our members will send to the Association the names of any stranger 
residing in the city, and we shall be glad to extend them an invitation and welcome 
them to the building. 

A luncheon was also held on Thanksgiving evening, at which fifty sat down 
to a hearty repast. An exceedingly pleasant and profitable evening was enjoyed 
by all. 

COMMITTEE MEN’s REUNIONS.—Three meetings, average attendance eighty. 
A new feature of our work, and one of great importance in the development 


O7 


of Committee men to a broad knowledge of Association work. Do our Committee 
men know who are on the other Committees, banded with them in the greatest 
Christian work in this world for young men? Do you grasp the whole idea of the 
Association movement ? Do not you need the prayers and advice of your fellow 
Committee men, and do not they need and appreciate your interest in their work ? 
Men have met with us whose lives are spent in Christ's service amongst young men— 
T. S. Cole, Claus Olandt, Jr., C. J. Hicks and David McConaughy, Jr.—lives like 
these would strengthen, ennoble and enrich your life. Do not miss a blessing along 
this line next year or lose an education in the work of the Association you serve. 
MEMBERS’ SOCIALS.—An opening social for members at the commencement of a 
busy fall’s work in October brought together over one thousand of our members and 


their friends. The programme was given in the centre hall, and the music was mu ch 
appreciated by those present. All class work was stopped, and the entire building 
was set aside for the use of the guests of the evening. 

The.Committee then turned their attention to the New Year’s Reception, and 
though this Reception and evening entertainment has always been a strong feature 
of social work for the year, it may fairly be said that 1896 was ushered in at 
the Association Rooms brighter and better than any year up to date. The 
Committee had carefully planned the decorations, and with the help of a number of 
our members who gladly rendered assistance, the building assumed, if possible, 
a more cheerful and beautiful aspect than ever before. A picture gallery, amateur 
photography and camera exhibit were among the new features, and though a first 
attempt, they show that it was a move in the right direction. Another new feature 


CT} pane st: 


38 


was the championship contest in the swimming bath, while the programme, on the 
yymnasium floor as usual, attracted more visitors than could be well accommodated. 
By actual count, over twenty-three hundred entered the building and partook of the 
welcome of the Association. The ladies in charge of the parlors and meeting rooms, 


where refreshments were daintily served, received the guests in the name of the 


Association. The large Reception Hall was constantly crowded by those who 
listened to the music of the Association Orchestra, of which we are justly proud. 

The evening concert drew an overflowing audience, was first class in every 
respect, and closed the most successful New Year’s Day Reception that our 
Association has ever held. 

The Social to have been held in February was postponed on account of the 
uncertainty of the date of our Anniversary Meeting. 

The April Social and the closing of the Educational classes were combined. The 
programme was given in the large hall, a number of the members of the different 
classes taking part, the music being under the charge of Mr. P. J. Illsley, assisted by 
the choir boys of St. George’s Church. Specimens of Freehand, Mechanical and 
Architectural Drawing, Penmanship, Phonography and Book-keeping were on 
exhibit in the reading rooms, while the ladies of Knox, Stanley and Douglas 
churches served refreshments in the parlors. - 

Your Committee are pleased to see a large increase in the attendance at these 
social gatherings, and trust that the efforts of those who so kindly take part in. 
the programme, and of the ladies in charge of the refreshments, will be as fully 
appreciated, as they are cheerfully and generously given, and that these evenings will 
be greatly looked forward to by our members. 

EVENING RECEPTION.—The Evening Reception Committee was organized for the 
season in the latter part of August, and has continued to do very fair work up to this | 
time. Several of the members have been compelled to drop out for one reason. 
and another, and sometimes it has been hard to fill their places. However, ° 
new men have been enlisted from time to time, and, on the whole, the majority 
of evenings have been supplied. 

The Committee assisted at each of the social evenings through the season, namely, 
the Fall Reunion, Oct. 22, the New Year’s Reception, and the Educatlonal | 
Closing, April 16. ! 

In closing we wish to express our pleasure at the prompt and kind response . 
we have had at all times to our request for assistance from the ladies, the orchestra 
and the many who have taken part in the programmes and enabled our members to 
enjoy such bright, attractive and, we trust, profitable evenings. 


JOHN W. ROSS, 
Chairman. 


EMPLOYMENT. 


Perhaps in no feature of the Association’s work is it more difficult to give 
an accurate report than this. So often it is a case of ‘‘ Were there not ten cleansed, 
but where are the nine?” Men counselled and assisted to employment, in many 
cases, fail to inform us concerning their success or non-success, and our report, 
therefore, cannot be so full as we would like. 

378 men filed applications for employment. 


og 


39 of these secured employment directly through the Association. 
74 succeeded by their own efforts. 

A regular portion of time is devoted each week day (except Saturday) to this 
work. Counsel and information is freely given to each man, and every means in our 
power taken to assist him in his need. Frequent encouragement has been had 
in spiritual dealing, and opportunity is here taken to present the Gospel to men who 


might not otherwise be easily reached. 
C. K. CALHOUN, 


Assistant Secretary. 


PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT. 


For the first time in our history we are unable to report an increase in 
numbers over the previous year. Although the enrolment has not been as large, the 
attendance has been more regular; and while some of the classes have fallen off, 
others have increased, so that, on the whole, we are not much below last year, which 
was the best season we ever had. 

The following are the figures for this Department :-— 


491 registered for the Gymnasium Classes. 
21 Classes held weekly. 


40) 


Class Averages:— Advanced —60 Sesssions. Attendance, 9 
Intermediate —64 aS ne 15 
Elementary —6I ae ef 30 
Students —58 py oe 20 
Business Men —50 “3 = 17 
Pastors —59 g ee 9 


Boys and Juniors—See Junior Department report. 
Physical Examinations.—294 young men, 74 boys—368. 


Total since opening, 2,641. 


In addition, many have been re-examined. 


At the close of last season Mr. H. H. Field resigned his position as Assistant 
Physical Director. We were very much pleased to be able to secure Mr. C. B. 
Powter, after his year’s study at the Springfield Training School, to fill the vacancy. 

A corps of 25 Volunteer L.eaders have rendered inestimable service by assisting Mr. 
Ball with the Gymnasium Classes. 

We extend our hearty thanks to Drs. W. H. Drummond, W. Grant Stewart, 
R. C. Kirkpatrick, and D. J. Evans, our Medical Examiners, for their interest and 
help in this Department. 

The apparatus and plant are in good condition. The Director’s Office has 
been enlarged, thus giving better facilities for conducting the Physical Examinations. 
The Gymnasium has been separated from the passage to the Bowling Alleys 


TS 


4] 


by a wire partition, which has proven a decided improvement. A _ diving 
platform was erected in the Swimming Bath, and is much appreciated by the 
members. 

BOWLING ALLEYS.—The Bowling Alleys have been used more than ever before. 
Individual contests for weekly, monthly and yearly prizes have been held. The 
Team Tournament was won by the St. George’s. Mr. S. W. McGarity, a member 
of the St. George’s, won the yearly: prize—a diamond triangle pin—by making 
an average of 246. He also holds the record score of the Alleys, having made 279. 


BAskET BALL.—Basket Ball has been played, and maintains its popularity. 
Several games have been played with outside teams in addition to tournaments 
among the young men and boys. | 

NEW FEATURES.—Two new features were added to the indoor work. In con- 
nection with the New Year’s Day programme, an all-round swimming championship 
contest was held, consisting of five different events, and conducted on the Pentathlon 
plan. The contest was won by Mr. H. Sharpe. 

The members of the Board of Directors offered a beautiful silver shield for an 
indoor Pentathlon contest. Several preliminaries were held, the final resulting in 
G. A. McBean scoring 398, H. P. Archibald and E. Roberts each 385. The names 
and score of these young men have been engraved on the shield, which will be 
hung permanently in the Association rooms. 

Both of these new features have been very successful, and will undoubtedly become 
annual fixtures. 


OUTDOOR WORK. 


ATHLETIC FIELD.--Your Committee feel that the possession of an Athletic 
Field is an -absolute need, which should receive immediate attention. The 
work of the winter in the Building is largely undone during the summer, because we 
cannot retain the interest of the members during the outdoor season, as they scatter 
among the various clubs of the city and in many instances fail to return in the fall. 

We have carefully considered this matter, have examined several pieces of land, 
and know of a suitable place for the purpose that can be purchased and equipped for 
about $10,000. We believe this to be an exceptional opportunity, but cannot take 
advantage of it unless some friend gives us a good start. 

Last year we were able to rent the old Shamrock Grounds from the National 
A.A.A. for three mornings and ove evening each week. This was greatly appreciated 
by a large number of the members. 


LACROSSE.—Considerable interest was shown in lacrosse, and the early morning 
practices were very well attended. No matches were played as we could not 
secure grounds for Saturday afternoon games. 


RucGBy.—Rugby football was played with great enthusiasm during September and 
October. As the other city clubs practised in the mornings, we were able to 
arrange several practice matches, winning three and losing only one by a single point. 


BICYCLE CLUB.—The most successful feature of the outdoor work has been the 


Bicycle Club, which has grown steadily in numbers and interest. Captain Manhire 
is the right man in the position, and keeps every member of the Club interested. 


42 


The boys say they are going to have the best Club in the city. The large portrait of 
the ‘Club on Mount Royal” in the Reception Hall is the gift of the members 
to the Association. 

ATHLETICS.—The vacant lot next to the Building has been a very attractive part 
of the summer work. A tennis court has been laid out and several tournaments 
played. Jumping, pole vaulting, running, quoits, basket ball and kindred games. 
have also been played. 

SUMMER CaMpP.—The summer camp at Ste. Agathe has proved a decided success. 
Last year the camp was open, with a cook and tents in attendance, during the entire 
months of July and August. This has become one of the most popular attractions. 
during the warm weather, and steps are being taken to erect a house as soon 
as possible. 

SNOW-SHOEING.—The interest in snow-shoeing is growing less and less each 
year. Nevertheless, the Club had several fine tramps, and the Veteran’’ and Ladies’ 
night, as well as the ** At Home,” were the best the Club ever had. 

Our Association was among the first to connect itself with the Athletic League of 
the Young Men’s Christian Associations of North America. 

WM. TEES, 
Chairman. 


JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 


The opportunity presented in the Junior Department is one of great responsibility 
and of equally great value to the Association. While-in the general work the 
Association ministers largely to the young men away from home, in the Junior 
Department the Association touches more largely the homes of the city, and is able 
to bring its influence to bear on the lives of the boys at an early age. 

The work of the past year may be briefly reviewed under the following heads :~ | 

(1.) SPIRITUAL.—The emphasis is placed here. While every encouragement is. 
given to hearty enjoyment in the way of safe companionship, good habits of reading, 
physical exercise and athletics, yet the chief stress is laid upon the need of knowing 
the Lord Jesus Christ as a personal Saviour, and any work that falls short of 
this ideal so far lacks vitality and permanence. . 

The Friday night meeting has continued to be the rallying point of the religious. 
work. The average attendance for the year, including the summer months, has been 
46. The Christian life is presented here from week to week, and the matter 
of decision for Christ is wisely urged from time to time. ‘There have been frequent 
enquirers, and we believe that quite a number of boys have begun the Christian life in 
connection with this service. 

Bible study has been encouraged. Two Bible Training Classes met regularly each 
Sunday afternoon during the fall and winter months, and in the latter part of 
the winter a third class was formed for boys who could not attend the other classes. 
The aim has been to promote systematic study of God’s Word, and to develop. 
leaders amongst the Christian boys who would be able to influence others to Christ. 
In addition, the Scripture-Union Card has been: widely circulated. It provides. 


43 


a course of regular daily readings, which, in a short time, enables those following it 
to cover the entire Bible. So far this year we have 60 members in the Union. 

The monthly service at the General Hospital has been maintained regularly and is 
deeply appreciated by the patients. We believe that the singing of the Gospel 
hymns in the wards will be the means of leading many to the Saviour. 

Several of the boys are regular contributors to the Extension Fund, and are thus 
beginning to take a practical interest in foreign missionary work that will be of great 
blessing in years to come. 

(2.) PHysIcAL.—In the line of indoor work, the Gymnasium and Baths have had 
an extensive use. The attendance has not been quite so large as in the earlier years, 
but the interest shown by the boys has been healthy. Examinations for promotion 


are being introduced this year in connection with the floor class work. It is believed 
that greater accuracy and interest in the exercises ou the part of the boys will result. 
Variety was lent to the work by the Basket Ball Tournament, lasting from December 
to April. 

In the line of outdoor work, several paper chases over the mountain were held 
during the fine weather of the early fall. The Snow-shoe Club was re-organized at 
the beginning of the winter, and tramped each Saturday afternoon, when the weather 
permitted, six times in all. The new feature this year was the selection of a different 
route for the tramp each week. The Annual Sleigh Drive, held in February, was a 
thorough success, and proved to be one of the most enjoyable events of the season. 
This-spring: has.seen.theeformation -of.a»Junior. Bicycle Club, which promises well. 


44 


All these outdoor features have the immense benefit of adding to the social life of 
the boys by enabling the members to get acquainted in a way that even the 
intercourse in the Building does not permit. 

The summer camp at St. Agathe was held again last summer, and was an entire 
success ; 22 members and leaders were out. 

(3.) SoctaL.—In this phase of the Department, perhaps, the least activity 
has been displayed. Two receptions were held—one on Dec. 4th to members, and 
one on April 13th to the members and _ their parents. Both were thoroughly 
enjoyed and successful. On Sept. 23 a re-union of the Committees took place, 
which did much to stimulate the work at the opening of the season.. On Nov. 30 we 
were favored with a visit from Mr. David McConaughy, of Madras, India, when a 
number of our workers had tea with him. A more intimate acquaintance with the 
foreign work was thus formed. The use of the Reading Room, Library and games 
has been about the same as last year. We very much need a better equipment both 
in additions of books to the Library and in the furnishings of the rooms. We 
confidently look for enlargement on these lines in the coming year. 

In conclusion, we are thankful for God’s blessing which, we believe, has rested 
upon the work the past year. We are thankful for the opportunities which 
have come to us daily for helpfulness to the young lives in the Junior membership, 
and though too few of these opportunities have been accepted, we pray for increasing 
wisdom and grace to enable us to follow them up closely that the name of our Father 
in heaven may be glorified.

EXTENSION FUND. 


This Fund is applied to the extension of Association work ontside our own 
city, and consists mainly of regular envelope contributions. Last year we reported 
30 contributors. Of these 12. have removed or discontinued, but 33 have been 
added, so that our present number of contributors is 51. As most of the new con- 
tributors were secured late in the year, our total contributions are slightly less than 
last year, but the prospects are that next year they will be greatly increased. 

During the year we have been visited by Messrs. Hicks and Olandt, of the 
International Committee, and by our Provincial Secretary, Mr. Cole, also by Mr. 
David McConaughy, Jr., the General Secretary for India, whose visit was a great 
blessing to many of us, and gave us a better idea of the extent and value of the work 
in India, to which the greater part of our fund is applied. Two interesting 
facts concerning the outside work are the securing of a building for the Madras, 
India, Association, and the completion of the new dormitory for the Springfield 
Training School. 

Our financial statement and list of contributors is as follows :—
